issues.legal_issue: The amount and form of permanent maintenance must reflect the parties’ financial circumstances, needs, status, and other relevant circumstances.
material_facts: The wife had worked as an air hostess before the marriage and resigned from that job after the marriage at the husband’s instance.
At the time of the maintenance claim, the wife was not permanently employed, had no regular income, and was living with her sister without immovable property of her own in that city.
The wife described her subsequent work and earnings as casual and irregular; the Court accepted her explanation.
The husband earned a salary as a senior commander, had properties in his name, and had future employment prospects.
The husband had remarried, had a child, and was responsible for looking after his parents.
The lower courts had fixed monthly maintenance at Rs. 20,000, which the Supreme Court found inadequate.
issues.conclusion: The Court increased monthly maintenance to Rs. 40,000, payable from the date of the application, with arrears payable in instalments. Alternatively, the husband could pay Rs. 40 lakhs as a lump sum, which would forfeit the wife’s claims. The husband could choose either mode, and the parties could seek variation if circumstances changed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 25 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, the court must determine a just amount by considering the respondent’s income and property, the applicant’s income and property, the parties’ conduct, and the other circumstances of the case. There is no fixed formula. The award should allow reasonable comfort consistent with the applicant’s status and former mode of life, while taking account of the respondent’s reasonable expenses and legal obligations to others and avoiding an excessive award. The Court relied on Shri Bhagwan Dutt v. Smt. Kamla Devi and Anr., (1975) 2 SCC 386, concerning a modest standard of living consistent with family status and consideration of the wife’s separate income and the husband’s earnings and commitments, and Chaturbhuj v. Sita Bai, (2008) 2 SCC 316, concerning a wife’s ability to maintain herself and the standard of living consistent with the family’s status.

rule.if: spousal_maintenance_proceeding and (applicant_lacks_regular_income or applicant_income_is_insufficient) and applicant_resigned_from_work_after_marriage_at_spouse_instance and applicant_had_prior_employment_status and respondent_has_substantial_income_or_property and respondent_has_other_financial_obligations

predicates.spousal_maintenance_proceeding: A spouse sought permanent maintenance in proceedings arising from the marriage or its dissolution.
predicates.applicant_lacks_regular_income: The applicant had no regular income or had income insufficient to meet reasonable needs.
predicates.applicant_resigned_from_work_after_marri: The applicant gave up employment after marriage at the other spouse’s instance.
predicates.applicant_had_prior_employment_status: The applicant had an employment history and a prior standard of life relevant to assessing reasonable support.
predicates.respondent_has_substantial_income_or_pro: The respondent had income, property, or employment prospects relevant to the ability to provide support.
predicates.respondent_has_other_financial_obligatio: The respondent had responsibilities to support other family members.

issues.definition: When a spouse seeks permanent maintenance, the applicant has insufficient regular income and gave up work after marriage at the other spouse’s instance, and the respondent has relevant financial means and obligations, the award is adjusted to provide reasonable support with a lump-sum alternative.
